slides.title:
Building Data and Sensing
for the Grimes Twin
slides.subtitle: Draft for discussion
slides.notes: This is a short update and discussion about data for the Grimes digital twin. First, this week's updates and what we need: campus energy data, the facilities follow-up and the Quest 3 test. Then the background: what building data Grimes already has, which sensors from Professor Soga's lab could add, a small pilot, and what it would look like in the twin.

slides.footnote: Grimes BAS vendor unconfirmed; campus controls standard (Div. 25) not found publicly.
slides.notes: The campus energy dashboard currently reads the Obvius meter loggers on Building Manager Online, BMO: whole-building electricity, water and steam every 15 minutes. On October 26 Facilities told us that BMO is no longer their source of truth: the platform is outdated and new meter points cannot be added. They recommend SkySpark, which they actively manage, and they are setting up an intake form so students can pull hourly data themselves. So the meter side of the dashboard will move to SkySpark. These are utility meters, not a building automation system. The campus standard for building automation is Automated Logic WebCTRL over BACnet, and new projects use it, so Grimes very likely has it, but we have not confirmed that. If it exists it would add temperatures, airflow, CO2, valve positions and equipment status. Access needs a CalNet login, an operational need and a Facilities work order, which may be charged back. What we need: first SkySpark access for the meter data, then a read-only trend export, the point list and the sequences of operation, tagged to equipment so each point can link to a BIM element ID.

slides.title: Sensing
slides.subtitle: Options, how fiber and MEMS sensing work, one pilot, and how it would look in the twin
slides.notes: Part three: test installs. A real case, then five small trials, each on a real BIM element.

slides.title: Sensing options for Grimes
slides.subtitle: From Prof. Soga’s lab and the CE170/278 course, ranked by fit for Grimes

rows: Leaks as warm or cold spots, ~1 m apart; radiant-loop faults
Pump, fan and pipe vibration level and spectrum
Battery life; radio through floors; IT approval
Flow noise, water hammer, pump harmonics along the riser
Data volume (kHz per metre); building noise

slides.footnote: Lab track record (tunnels, pipelines, piles): Crossrail, EBMUD Hayward Fault pipe, PG&E gas pipe, Millennium Tower. No operating-building MEP deployment found. Concepts: CE170/278 Infrastructure Sensing, UC Berkeley (Prof. K. Soga).
slides.notes: These are the sensing options from Professor Soga's lab and the CE170/278 infrastructure sensing course, ranked for Grimes. Fiber temperature sensing along pipes is the best fit: it shows leaks as warm or cold spots and can reveal radiant loop faults, but the analyzer is costly and the cable needs routing. Wireless vibration nodes are easy and commercial, though battery life, radio through floors and IT approval are limits. Fiber vibration sensing on risers is research grade for leaks. Fiber Bragg grating sensors only measure known points, so they miss leaks elsewhere. Indoor environment nodes mostly duplicate points the building automation system already has. The lab's own track record is in tunnels, pipelines and piles; we found no operating-building MEP deployment, which is the gap this project would fill.

slides.notes: This is the first test, on the same location as test install one: the sprinkler main, Pipe219763. Run a fiber cable along it. The analyzer gives a temperature about every meter along the cable. We map each cable distance to a BIM pipe segment, so the temperature shows on that pipe in the twin viewer. Then we apply a contained, controlled thermal test, with the method agreed with Facilities. The success criterion is concrete: the test temperature change is detected and located on the correct BIM segment, and a wetness sensor below checks for water. It also tests the whole chain from sensor to BIM element to viewer. We need Facilities approval, access to the pipe, a safe way to apply the test change, a loan of a DTS analyzer, and reference temperatures to compare against.
slides.takeaway: One pipe, one cable, one contained test, with a stated pass criterion.

slides.footnote: Concept mockup — no sensors are installed; values are illustrative. Base: public Lens overlay of the May 6, 2026 capture (own screenshot); graphics added.
slides.notes: This is a concept of how the sensors would look in the twin. The base is the public Lens overlay of the Level 1 leak ceiling from the May 6 capture. Nothing is installed and the values are made up. Marker one is the fiber temperature line, coloured from blue for cool to red for hot along the sprinkler main. Marker two is an alert ring where the line is warmer than expected, which could mean a leak. Marker three is a wireless vibration node, and marker four is a leak sensor on the tile below the warm spot, to confirm water. It would work in three steps. The analyzer reports a temperature at a distance along the cable. We map that distance to a BIM pipe element ID using a survey of the cable route. Then the viewer colours that pipe and shows the alert, both in the Lens on the computer and in the headset.
